title: Nakamura Widens Lead In Esports World Cup Qualification Standings
summary:
The 2026 Salesforce FIDE World Championship also began on November 24, but Titled Tuesday continued apace, with its ongoing role in qualification for one of next year's biggest chess competitions, the 2027 Esports World Cup (EWC). GM Hikaru Nakamura won, scoring 9.5/11 for the victory on tiebreaks ahead of GMs Alireza Firouzja and Andrey Esipenko.

Nakamura widened his already substantial lead in the 2026-27 Champions Chess Tour (CCT) Standings with the victory, which was his third of the year but his second in just the last six weeks.

CCT Standings

In addition to their points from Titled Tuesday, Nakamura and GM Denis Lazavik also have at least 30 points from victories in the first round of Speed Chess Championship XI. More are possible if they advance farther, and some other players will also get extra points as SCC matches continue.

Unlike last year's CCT events, top finishers in the SCC and Chess.com Open aren't guaranteed a spot in the EWC beyond what their points entitle them to. The top 12 qualify.

Broadcast

There was no Chess.com broadcast of Titled Tuesday this week because of the world championship. Nakamura streamed on his Kick channel and then recapped game one of the world championship for YouTube; the latter is below.

Recap

Rounds 1-4

Nakamura was in fine playing form early after some small difficulty in the first round, becoming one of 14 players on 4/4. Firouzja and Esipenko had achieved the same score. Among Nakamura's victories was an underpromotion in the third round that induced instant resignation from FM Yan Domin after just 21 moves.

Round 5

While Nakamura lost in the fifth round to IM Renato Terry, Esipenko and Firouzja's success continued in the next round. Firouzja defeated GM Bardiya Daneshvar with the devastating 31.Nf6+. As Domin could only do against Nakamura's last move of round three, Daneshvar resigned.

Rounds 6

By now, just six perfect players remained, and that number would dwindle to two by the end of round six, after Terry and Firouzja made a draw. Terry played a great game, but slipped near the end to allow perpetual check. The players to successfully reach 6/6 were Esipenko and, after a bizarre blunder by his opponent, IM Kirill Klukin.

Round 7

Naturally, they were matched up in the seventh round, where Esipenko got to play White and won cleanly, without any need for dramatics.

Elsewhere, Firouzja just needed 19 moves to get back into the win column against IM Pawel Sowinski, while the near-opposite happened in Terry's game as he lost a time scramble against GM Jose Martinez. Meanwhile, Nakamura kept his recovery going with a second straight win, while GM Fabiano Caruana pulled off his sixth in a row to join Firouzja and Martinez on 6.5/7.

Round 8

To defend his perfect score, Esipenko now had to face Firouzja, but did get White. Caruana had White versus Martinez, and Nakamura was back up to board three against GM Ray Robson. The Esipenko–Firouzja game concluded bloodlessly, allowing the perfect score bounty to survive yet another tournament unscathed and move to $6,750 next week. Over in the Americas, Caruana seemed to be heading for a win, but Martinez took it from him in time trouble, while Nakamura was struggling to the point of referring to himself in the third person, but Robson soon was the one to run out of time.

Round 9

That left Martinez and Esipenko the only players on 7.5/8 entering the final break of the tournament. Martinez would end up getting the better of their matchup coming out of it, advancing into the sole lead. Behind him, however, Nakamura and Firouzja kept up the pressure and reached 8/9. Against FM Artin Ashraf, Nakamura missed a mate-in-one, but was so far ahead it didn't matter, while Firouzja soundly defeated GM Zhamsaran Tsydypov.

Round 10

Nakamura and Firouzja both faced tough matches in the 10th round, taking Black against Martinez and Caruana, respectively. Yet both won, making themselves coleaders with one round to go. Nakamura credited himself with an "impressive squeeze" to get the win out of a position that looked drawn for some time, and knock Martinez from his perch.

Round 11

Espying his tiebreaks, Nakamura was pessimistic about his winning chances, especially after he took the black pieces in his final round. Because of the latter fact, Nakamura played cautiously, and an extremely uneventful draw followed. But Nakamura's tiebreaks were closer than he thought, and the draw put him on the brink of winning.

Esipenko, facing Terry with both of them on 8.5 points, was already up 51 seconds on the clock when Terry took another 38 ticks to play the losing move.

Martinez also had a chance to move up to 9.5 points, but he could only stalemate GM Sina Movahed. Nine points were still enough to finish fourth with better tiebreaks than two IMs, Aleksandr Usov in fifth and Havard Haug in sixth.

Nakamura assumed he hadn't won until the end-of-tournament standings popped up on his screen; he ultimately beat out Firouzja by two tiebreak points and Esipenko by six. Nakamura readily admitted to improved play in recent Titled Tuesdays, which he credited to two things: playing more serious openings and using more time judiciously (instead of playing quickly and, his words, "trying to cheese on the clock" at the end of games). The new strategies are clearly helping, and his presence at the 2027 Esports World Cup is already nearly assured.

title: Mizzou Defeats UTD In Tiebreaks To Win Collegiate Chess League
summary:
The University of Missouri (Mizzou) defeated the defending champions, University of Texas at Dallas (UTD) in an exciting final match of the Collegiate Chess League Fall 2026 (CCL). Mizzou couldn't hold onto their early lead, allowing the match to reach an 8-8 tie, leading to a winner-takes-all tiebreak match. In the tiebreaks, Mizzou swept all four games to take their first title since the Fall 2024 season.

Mizzou edged UTD in a tight final match.

Round One

In the first round, Mizzou took a decisive lead, winning three games and drawing one. GM Aryan Tari got off to a good start, winning with Black against GM Sankalp Gupta.

Round Two

In the second round, UTD struck back, winning three games, drawing one, and evening the score. Gupta got back on track with a well-played win against GM Mahel Boyer.

Round Three

After two back-and-forth rounds, the the match settled down in round three. Boyer won for Mizzou, while Gupta won again for UTD. GM Aditya Samant had a great chance to score another critical point, but allowed Tari to slip away, keeping the match tied.

Round Four

For the second-straight round, neither side was able to break through in round four. Each team won two games, including this powerful performance by GM Rahul Srivatshav against Tari.

Tiebreaks

In the regular season, the match would have ended 8-8, but the CCL doesn't allow co-champions. The teams played one final round and Mizzou absolutely dominated. They won cleanly on every board to take the match 12-8. Boyer scored the final point to take the title.

You can watch the final match, hosted by Joe Lee.

The Collegiate Chess League is the premier online chess competition for college students.

title: Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match: A draw in the opening game
summary: Javokhir Sindarov and Gukesh Dommaraju drew their first encounter in the Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 in Geneva. Both players produced a highly accurate performance in a complex game, with neither managing to tilt the balance decisively in their favour. The tension was palpable at the Fondation Martin Bodmer as the first game of the long-awaited match between reigning World Champion Gukesh D and his challenger Javokhir Sindarov was about to get underway. The two contenders shook hands a few minutes before the start and settled into their respective seats, ready to concentrate fully on the battle ahead. Following a brief introduction by moderator Maurice Ashley, the traditional ceremonial first moves were made by FIDE President Timur Turlov and FIDE Deputy President and five-time World Champion Viswanathan Anand. Mr Turlov played 1.e4 on behalf of Sindarov, while Mr Anand responded with 1…e5 for his compatriot Gukesh. Whether they had guessed the players’ intentions correctly or had been given a little insider information, we shall probably never know. In any case, both contenders opted for the classical opening par excellence: 1.e4 e5. In a Ruy Lopez Opening, Gukesh employed the extremely solid Berlin Defence. This variation rose to prominence after Vladimir Kramnik used it to great effect against Garry Kasparov in their 2000 World Championship match. There is little doubt that both contenders had analyzed this opening extensively well before the match. Interestingly, only Gukesh previously had once ventured into the famous queenless middlegame arising after the exchanges 6.Bxc6 and 8.Qxd8, and he did so with the white pieces. At the post-game press conference, Sindarov explained that he had deliberately opted for a solid approach in the opening game, allowing himself to settle into the match and get a feel for the atmosphere in the playing hall. Speaking of the latter, both players expressed their satisfaction with the playing conditions at the Fondation Martin Bodmer and welcomed the presence of a select group of spectators following the action from the gallery. Later in the game, Gukesh began to invest considerable time around move 15 before coming up with a neat plan involving the advance of his a-pawn, followed by 17…Bb4 and 18…h6. This effectively prevented his opponent from launching an initiative with Nd4. Sindarov later explained that he had tried to generate attacking chances on the kingside with the manoeuvre 19.Ng3, followed by Nh5 and a pawn advance with g4 and f4. Both players subsequently revealed that they had been reasonably optimistic about their respective chances. The Uzbek GM eventually succeeded in opening lines against his opponent’s king, but Gukesh remained firmly in control with the precise 27…Kf6, a move that Sindarov admitted he had underestimated. The challenger quickly regrouped, however, and found a series of accurate moves that ultimately led to a repetition and a draw on move 38. A solid and well-fought opening encounter, with the match score now standing at 0.5–0.5. FACT SHEET, Game 1, Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026: White: Javokhir SindarovBlack: Gukesh DommarajuResult: ½-½Opening: Ruy Lopez, Berlin DefenceGame length: 38 movesMatch score: ½-½ Gukesh will have the white pieces in the second game, scheduled for Wednesday, November 25, at 3 p.m. at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, Geneva. Chess beyond the playing hall Although the World Championship Match is unquestionably the main attraction, FIDE has also put together an extensive programme of side events for chess fans visiting Geneva. Most of these activities take place in the fan zone, situated just a few hundred metres from the Fondation Martin Bodmer, in the heart of Cologny. The first major attraction got underway just half an hour into the game, when Viswanathan Anand took to the stage to explain the opening moves to the public and share anecdotes from his numerous World Championship encounters. The atmosphere in the spacious fan zone was already buzzing, with spectators, event hosts and volunteers contributing to a genuine celebration of chess. Another highlight gave visitors the opportunity to take on former Women’s World Champion Alexandra Kosteniuk in a consultation game. The audience had two minutes to discuss and vote on each move, and the resulting encounter kept everyone entertained for a full two hours before eventually ending in a draw. The full programme of side events accompanying the World Championship Match can be found on the official championship website. Written by Yannick Pelletier Photos: Y.E. Nisenbaum and Michal Walusza The Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 is taking place at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, near Geneva, Switzerland, from November 22 to December 12. The first round was played on November 24. All information on the schedule can be found on the Championship website. Tickets to the playing hall and the fan zone can be purchased on the designated website: https://tickets.fide.com/en , while games can be watched on the FIDE YouTube channel with live commentaries by top Grandmasters Peter Leko and Peter Svidler.

title: World Junior Championship U20 Championship 2026 at midpoint: India tops the standings in both sections
summary: Following the sixth round of the 2026 World Junior U20 Championship in Caracas, top-seeded Indian IM Ethan Vaz (pictured below) leads the Open tournament with a perfect score of six wins from six games. IMs Santiago López (COL) and Khagan Ahmad (AZE) are tied for second place with 5/6. Standings after Round 6 – Open Strong performances by home players Among the highest-ranked Venezuelans in the competition – which brings together the elite of the U20 chess world – are Santiago Ortega from Táchira, in 14th place, and Sebastián Borges from Miranda, in 15th place. Venezuelan International Master Juan Röhl highlighted the performance of both home players, stating that they have lived up to expectations in the tournament. He noted that sound strategies and effective energy management, with the support of their coaches, will be key to both players securing a place among the world’s top 10 or 20 in the category once the tournament concludes. “They are two major talents. Santiago Ortega has stood out for several years and is once again delivering a strong performance. Sebastián has been making steady progress; he has been a national champion in several age categories and has recently performed very well in various events. In fact, he is improving his international ranking and putting in a strong showing in this junior championship with four points out of six,” he said. Saviha consolidates her lead in the Girls section Meanwhile, in the Girls’ section, India’s IM Savitha Shri B is in the sole lead with a perfect 6/6. WIM Diana Khafizova (RUS), WFM V.C. Nivedita (IND), FM Chen Yining (CHN), and WIM Anna Laura Scarsi (ARG) share second place, trailing the leader by 1.5 points. Standings after Round 6 – Girls CM Mariana Terán from the state of Trujillo, Venezuela, is currently ranked 12th with 4/6. “Mariana Terán was a member of the Olympiad team that competed in Uzbekistan. She is a player who is making clear progress and has had a very good tournament, scoring four points out of six, thanks to her sound theoretical preparation and positive mindset. We hope she performs well in the coming rounds,” said Röhl. “Other players from the national squad who have stood out in the event are Jesús Rivas from Miranda State and Ahyled Gil, both of whom are exceeding expectations. We are also looking forward to seeing FIDE Master and 2025 Open national champion Dilson Pérez, who competed in the Olympiad and is expected to finish the tournament on a high note, as well as Ana Escobar and Catherine Reyes, hoping they have a very successful second half of the tournament to improve their final rankings,” he added. Finally, Röhl stated that the 2026 World Junior U20 Championship in Caracas is a golden opportunity for the 41 Venezuelan players to gain greater experience in international events by playing high-level games against Grandmasters and achieving positive results. title: World Championship Game 1: A draw in the Berlin, not without tension
summary:
The World Chess Championship match between Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov got under way on Tuesday in Geneva, with the two 20-year-old contenders signing a draw in a tense 38-move encounter. Playing white, Sindarov obtained a considerable advantage on the clock in a Berlin Endgame. Gukesh, however, showed excellent defensive skills, finding precise moves under time pressure to keep the balance. | Photo: FIDE / Michal Walusza

Gukesh under pressure

What remains the most popular event in the chess calendar, particularly among mainstream audiences, got under way on Tuesday at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, near Geneva. The elegant setting is particularly fitting for an event with such a rich history, especially at a time when efforts to popularise the royal game increasingly revolve around fast-paced competitions, often played online or on computers in front of a live audience.

It has been 140 years since Wilhelm Steinitz became the first officially recognised world chess champion, in 1886, and the tradition lives on. Eighteen players have held the undisputed world title, with Gukesh Dommaraju, the defending champion in Geneva, the latest addition to the list. Coincidentally, Gukesh was 18 years old when he defeated Ding Liren to become the youngest undisputed world chess champion in history.

Gukesh now faces Javokhir Sindarov in what is, by average age, the youngest World Championship match in history, with both contenders aged 20. Sindarov will celebrate his 21 st birthday on 8 December, the day on which game 12 is scheduled to take place. Theoretically, the Uzbek grandmaster could claim the world title on his birthday, much as Magnus Carlsen did in 2016. The Norwegian secured his third victory in a match for the crown by defeating Sergey Karjakin in rapid tiebreaks on 30 November, the day he turned 26.

The first game of the match is under way at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny | Photo: Michal Walusza

Three chess legends commentating on the game - Peter Svidler, Vishy Anand and Peter Leko | Photo: Michal Walusza

As determined by the drawing of colours at Sunday's opening ceremony, Sindarov had the white pieces in the first game of the match. Following 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 , Gukesh opted for the Berlin Defence with 3...Nf6 , and Sindarov agreed to allow the much-explored Berlin Endgame by playing 4.0-0 instead of opting for the Anti-Berlin with 4.d3. Gukesh followed the main line, and the theoretical battle began.

The Berlin has a notable history in World Championship matches. Vladimir Kramnik famously employed the system to neutralise Garry Kasparov's formidable opening preparation in their 2000 match in London. Fourteen years later, in Sochi, Magnus Carlsen secured his second world title with a victory over Vishy Anand in game 11 of their match out of a Berlin. The Indian legend incorrectly sacrificed an exchange to obtain a passed pawn on the queenside.

In Geneva, Sindarov blitzed out his preparation up to and including 13.Ne4 , a novelty. Gukesh had already been playing at a more measured pace, and after spending over 15 minutes on his response to the new move, found himself 25 minutes behind on the clock.

A tense battle ensued, with Sindarov looking for ways to increase the pressure and Gukesh carefully dealing with the threats to maintain the balance. By the time Sindarov played 21.g4 , a move that was not the engines' first choice, the Uzbek had a 30-minute advantage on the clock. Gukesh had just 16 minutes to make 20 more moves, with no increments until after the first time control.

The tension continued to build, as tactical complications were becoming increasingly difficult to avoid. Sindarov soon sacrificed a pawn temporarily, and precise play was required from Gukesh to keep the position under control.

It was at this point that the Indian star demonstrated that the time he had invested earlier in the game had been well spent. Gukesh began to play quickly and confidently, clearly having worked out the critical lines in advance. Despite the considerable disparity on the clock, the defending champion gave his opponent little opportunity to make progress.

Sindarov eventually saw no benefit in playing on, and the game ended in a draw by threefold repetition on move 38.

Javokhir Sindarov incorrectly claimed a draw and was penalised by the arbiters (he lost two minutes on the clock) - but that was just a formality | Photo: Michal Walusza

At the post-game press conference, Gukesh explained that he felt he had things under control throughout the encounter and did not "really need to be worried". Sindarov, for his part, acknowledged that his opponent had "defended very well".

World number seven Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, who is rooting for his compatriot, summed up the encounter on X :

Incredible first game of World Championship match! High quality game from both! Gukesh found great moves under pressure!

title: World Chess Championship: A look at the international press
summary:
The World Chess Championship match between Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov has attracted considerable attention beyond the specialised chess media. The youth of the two contenders, their contrasting results over the past year and the psychological demands of a title match are among the recurring themes in the international coverage. Other articles explore Sindarov's personality, the unusual literary setting in Geneva and the relevance of human chess in the age of artificial intelligence. | Photo: FIDE / Michal Walusza

All eyes on Geneva

As is customary when the world title is at stake, chess has found its way into the sports and culture sections of major international publications. The encounter between Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov offers journalists a number of interesting angles, not least the contrasting trajectories of the two young grandmasters over the past twelve months.

Sunday's press conference and opening ceremony provided an opportunity for journalists to hear from both contenders. Gukesh's determination to approach the match as an opportunity to win the title anew, rather than as a title defence, was picked up by several publications. Meanwhile, the Uzbek media highlighted Sindarov's measured assessment of his chances.

Press conference and opening ceremony

The Guardian: Gukesh vows to win world chess title 'all over again' as Sindarov challenge looms

The Times of India: Gukesh vs Sindarov press conference: Who said what before World Chess Championship 2026

Kun.uz (Uzbekistan): Sindarov rates his chances against Gukesh at 50-50 ahead of world title match

ChessBase India: Gukesh vs Sindarov: Everything said at the World Championship 2026 press conference

Javokhir Sindarov and Gukesh Dommaraju were both interviewed by FIDE's Charlyze van Zyl ahead of the much-anticipated match | Photo: Michal Walusza

Much of the coverage in the run-up to the match has revolved around the question of how relevant recent form will prove to be in a head-to-head contest. Sindarov's remarkable progress and Gukesh's difficulties since becoming world champion have prompted several observers to favour the challenger. The Indian grandmaster's previous experience of a World Championship match, however, is by no means an insignificant factor.

Match previews

Reuters: Focus returns to the board as Gukesh defends world title against Sindarov

Financial Times: Chess: Sindarov odds on to win world crown in Geneva match

India Today: Gukesh's rocky reign meets Sindarov's remarkable rise in world title clash

Hindustan Times: D Gukesh vs Javokhir Sindarov: Fortitude meets form in battle for world chess crown

Al Jazeera: Gukesh vs Sindarov: The youngest World Chess Championship in history

US Chess: 2026 Salesforce FIDE World Championship Preview

Javokhir Sindarov will play white in game one | Photo: Michal Walusza

There is also plenty of reading material for those interested in aspects of the match other than the sporting contest itself. Bryan Armen Graham interviewed Sindarov for The Guardian, exploring, among other things, the Uzbek's competitive attitude towards his hobbies. Amit Kamath, writing for The Indian Express, took a closer look at the extraordinary collection of books surrounding the players at the Fondation Martin Bodmer.

From a rather different perspective, Canadian writer Stephen Marche uses the World Championship as a starting point for a reflection on artificial intelligence and the enduring appeal of human intellectual competition.

title: Kateryna Lagno wins inaugural WR Women's Chess Tour
summary:
Kateryna Lagno claimed the winner's trophy at the inaugural WR Women's Chess Tour 2026. She reached the final in both the rapid and the blitz section of the final tournament in Stuttgart but lost on both occasions. Nevertheless, her results were enough to secure overall victory in the inaugural tour organised by Wadim Rosenstein. Anna Muzychuk won the blitz tournament, while Carissa Yip came out on top in the rapid event. | Pictured: (from left to right): blitz winner Anna Muzychuk, overall winner Kateryna Lagno and rapid winner Carissa Yip | Photo: Lennart Ootes

Kateryna Lagno takes the title

The WR Women's Chess Tour, organised for the first time by Wadim Rosenstein in 2026, has come to an end and has its first winner: at the end of a tournament series that travelled through Manila, Tokyo, Bangkok and Hong Kong before reaching the final in Stuttgart, Kateryna Lagno emerged victorious.

The final tournament took place at Rosenstein Palace. As in the qualifying events, a blitz tournament was played on day one and a rapid tournament on day two, both in knockout format. The time controls were 3 minutes plus 2 seconds from move 1 in blitz, and 15 minutes plus 10 seconds from move 1 in rapid. The blitz competition was played over four games, while rapid was played over half that distance - with an Armageddon game deciding the match in the event of a tie.

The following players had qualified for the final tournament in the capital of Baden-Württemberg:

Day 1: Blitz tournament

The tournament opened with a match between the two Muzychuk sisters. After a draw in a rook endgame in the first game, an exciting battle developed in the four-game family duel.

"It was a little strange to travel all the way to Germany just to play my sister", said Mariya Muzychuk. "We could really have done that at home". | Photo: Lennart Ootes

After three wins for white, Anna had beaten Mariya 2½-1½ and thus qualified for the semifinal against Zhu Jiner. There, as well as in the final against Kateryna Lagno, Muzychuk won by the same score and secured victory in the blitz tournament. Muzychuk had gone 2-0 up and, after losing game 3, was able to hold the fourth game to a draw.

The blitz final between Kateryna Lagno and Anna Muzychuk | Photo: Sebastian Siebrecht

Lagno, who lost the final, had reached it by beating Vaishali Rameshbabu 2½-½ and Leya Garifullina 2½-1½.

Day 2: Rapid tournament

Carissa Yip had an opportunity for revenge at the start of the rapid tournament: the previous day, she had been eliminated straight away by Zhu Jiner, the world number two among women players. As in the blitz, an Armageddon game was required to decide the match. Yip won game one, Zhu the second. In the deciding game, Yip won with black. In the semifinal against Anna Muzychuk, the American scored a 1½-½ victory.

Yip's opponent in the final had to go to Armageddon twice to advance. She first eliminated Garifullina and then Mariya Muzychuk. With both Muzychuk sisters losing in the semifinals, there was no second family duel, which in this case would even have been the final.

Carissa Yip won the rapid tournament. Kateryna Lagno reached the final in both disciplines and thus secured overall victory. | Photo: Lennart Ootes

In the final, Yip won game one and was able to hold a draw in the next encounter, in which Lagno initially managed to obtain an advantage but could not convert it into a win.

Rosenstein Palace

Incidentally, the name Rosenstein Palace has nothing to do with the organiser's name, as explained on the tournament website: "Rosenstein Palace was built as a summer residence for King Wilhelm I of Württemberg according to plans by the Florentine court architect Giovanni Salucci. The foundation stone was laid in 1824, and the palace was inaugurated six years later. Rosenstein means rose rock. According to legend, the king chose this name because the rose was the favourite flower of his late wife, Queen Katharina. Since 1954, the palace has housed the biological collections of the State Museum of Natural History Stuttgart".
